---
title: "Errata for *A 2 million-person, campaign-wide field experiment shows how digital advertising affects voter turnout*"
format:
  pdf:
    output-file: aggarwal_etal_2023_errata.pdf
    toc: false
    number-sections: false
    geometry: margin=1in
---

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
library(tidyverse)
library(here)
here::i_am("errata.qmd")

gt <- read_csv(
  here::here("ground_truth", "aggarwal_etal_2023_ground_truth.csv"),
  col_types = cols(value_paper = col_character(), .default = col_guess())
)
extraction <- read_csv(
  here::here("ground_truth", "published_claims.csv"),
  col_types = cols(value_paper = col_character(), needs_block = col_logical(),
                   .default = col_guess())
)

# claim_id is never missing here, but indexing with a bare logical would return
# extra NA elements the moment one were, so every lookup asserts a single row.
value <- function(id, column = "value_rewrite") {
  row <- gt[!is.na(gt$claim_id) & gt$claim_id == id, ]
  stopifnot(nrow(row) == 1)
  row[[column]]
}

published <- function(id) {
  row <- extraction[extraction$claim_id == id, ]
  stopifnot(nrow(row) == 1)
  row$value_paper
}

number_word <- function(x) {
  words <- c("one", "two", "three", "four", "five", "six", "seven", "eight", "nine",
             "ten", "eleven", "twelve", "thirteen", "fourteen", "fifteen", "sixteen",
             "seventeen", "eighteen", "nineteen", "twenty", "twenty-one", "twenty-two",
             "twenty-three", "twenty-four")
  words[as.integer(x)]
}

with_commas <- function(x) format(round(as.numeric(x)), big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE)

# Monthly persuasion spending, from the figure the sentence describes.
monthly_spend <-
  read_csv(here::here("maintained", "output", "figure_b2_acronym_spending.csv"),
           show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  filter(panel == "Keyword") |>
  group_by(month) |>
  summarize(spend_lb = sum(spend_lb), .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(desc(spend_lb))

top_month <- format(monthly_spend$month[1], "%B")
top_spend <- with_commas(monthly_spend$spend_lb[1])
july_spend <- with_commas(monthly_spend$spend_lb[monthly_spend$month == as.Date("2020-07-01")])

n_covariates <- value("methods_n_covariates")
n_covariates_word <- number_word(n_covariates)

audience <- with_commas(published("methods_treatment_audience"))
eligible <- with_commas(published("methods_programme_eligible"))

omnibus_num_df <- value("methods_omnibus_df_first_subscript")
omnibus_den_df <- format(round(value("methods_omnibus_df_second_subscript")), scientific = FALSE)
omnibus_den_df_commas <- with_commas(value("methods_omnibus_df_second_subscript"))
omnibus_f <- sprintf("%.4f", value("methods_omnibus_f"))
omnibus_p <- sprintf("%.3f", value("methods_omnibus_p"))

wesleyan_share <- sprintf("%.2f", value("si_c_wesleyan_share"))
wesleyan_total <- with_commas(published("si_c_wesleyan_total"))
wesleyan_acronym <- with_commas(published("si_c_wesleyan_acronym"))
```

Five corrections to *Nature Human Behaviour* article `r "10.1038/s41562-022-01487-4"`. None of
them changes a conclusion of the article. Every corrected value below is computed at render time
from a full reproduction of the published analysis, held in the repository
`active-maintenance-aec/aggarwal_etal_2023`. Bold marks the tokens that changed; everything else
in each corrected sentence is the published wording.

## 1. The month of heaviest persuasion spending

> In fact, we observe significant early spending (Acronym spent more on persuasion in
> **July** than in any other month, see main Figure **??**), and we find much stronger effects on
> early voting than day of voting (see Figure 3 in the main text).

**Corrected:** In fact, we observe significant early spending (Acronym spent more on persuasion
in **`r top_month`** than in any other month, see **Supplementary Figure 2**), and we find much
stronger effects on early voting than day of voting (see Figure 3 in the main text).

The figure the sentence points at is Supplementary Figure 2, whose two panels split Acronym's
monthly lower-bound spending on persuasion advertisements by format and by keyword. Summed over
either panel's series, the largest month is `r top_month` 2020 at US\$`r top_spend`,
against US\$`r july_spend` in July. The cross-reference did not resolve when the document was
typeset. The sentence's argument, that Acronym spent heavily earlier in the campaign than other
left-leaning advertisers did, is unaffected: `r top_month` is earlier than July.

## 2. The number of pre-treatment covariates tested for balance

> As shown in Fig. 5, the random assignment procedure generated treatment and control groups that
> were balanced on pre-treatment characteristics in this subset. Out of **21** covariates, only two
> exhibited statistically significant imbalance.

**Corrected:** As shown in Fig. 5, the random assignment procedure generated treatment and control
groups that were balanced on pre-treatment characteristics in this subset. Out of
**`r n_covariates`** covariates, only two exhibited statistically significant imbalance.

Figure 5 plots `r n_covariates_word` covariates and Supplementary Table 3 prints
`r n_covariates_word` rows. The count of two significant imbalances is right, and so is
everything the paragraph goes on to say about them.

## 3. The size of the treatment audience

> The full cost of the advertising campaign was US\$8.9 million, spread out over a treatment
> audience of **`r audience` million** (`r eligible` programme-eligible voters × our 60% match
> rate), amounting to US\$4.46 of advertising expenditure per voter.

**Corrected:** The full cost of the advertising campaign was US\$8.9 million, spread out over a
treatment audience of **`r audience`** (`r eligible` programme-eligible voters × our 60% match
rate), amounting to US\$4.46 of advertising expenditure per voter.

The parenthetical states the arithmetic: `r eligible` times a 60 per cent match rate is
`r audience` people. The word "million" makes the figure a million times too large.

## 4. The degrees of freedom of the balance F test

> An F-test comparing a regression of treatment status on covariates with strata fixed effects
> versus a restricted model predicting treatment status from strata fixed effects was
> non-significant (F~**`r published("methods_omnibus_df_first_subscript")`,−18**~ =
> `r omnibus_f`; P = `r omnibus_p`).

**Corrected:** An F-test comparing a regression of treatment status on covariates with strata
fixed effects versus a restricted model predicting treatment status from strata fixed effects was
non-significant (F~**`r omnibus_num_df`,`r omnibus_den_df`**~ = `r omnibus_f`;
P = `r omnibus_p`).

An F statistic carries its numerator degrees of freedom first. The unrestricted model has
`r omnibus_num_df` more parameters than the restricted one and leaves `r omnibus_den_df_commas` residual
degrees of freedom. The published subscripts are the second row of the Wald test's printed
output, where the first figure is that model's residual degrees of freedom and the second is the
difference in parameters, printed as a negative number. The statistic and the p-value are right.

## 5. Acronym's share of federal advertising spending on Facebook

> According to this data, there was a total of approximately US\$`r wesleyan_total` spent on
> federal races on Facebook from 2/1/2020 to 11/3/2020, US\$`r wesleyan_acronym` (**0.67%**) of
> which was from Acronym.

**Corrected:** According to this data, there was a total of approximately US\$`r wesleyan_total`
spent on federal races on Facebook from 2/1/2020 to 11/3/2020, US\$`r wesleyan_acronym`
(**`r wesleyan_share`%**) of which was from Acronym.

A rounding artifact rather than a substantive error: the quotient of the sentence's own two
figures is `r sprintf("%.4f", value("si_c_wesleyan_share"))` per cent, which rounds up. The share
is kept at two decimal places because at one decimal the published and corrected figures are the
same.
